title: Installation & Architecture
subtitle: How a repurposed laptop became a SIEM, and the order everything got built in.

hardware.title: The hardware constraint that shaped everything
hardware.intro: The SIEM server ("soc-server") is a Toshiba Satellite C670D-12Q laptop — nothing close to what a production SIEM would run on. That constraint is deliberate: it forces every performance and reliability finding on this site to be real, not theoretical.

specs.label: CPU
specs.value: 2 cores, x86-64 — the single biggest bottleneck in the whole lab

specs.label: Boot method
specs.value: PXE/netboot install — the hardware can't boot from USB or DVD at all

architecture.intro: A mix of physical hardware and VirtualBox VMs, deliberately spanning three operating systems and including both an "attacker" box and an out-of-original-scope macOS addition — to demonstrate awareness of coverage gaps rather than hide them.

order.title: Onboarding a new machine: the actual checklist used
order.intro: Every machine in the lab follows the same sequence, documented once and reused instead of re-derived each time.

steps.title: 1. Connect it to Wazuh
steps.text: Configure networking (Bridged mode for VMs, not NAT — otherwise the machine never lands on the real LAN subnet), test connectivity to the manager on ports 1514/1515, check for a leftover agent registration from a prior image (this alone caused rework on almost every reused VM), then run the dashboard-generated install command. Only move on once the agent shows Active.

steps.title: 2A. Windows → Sysmon
steps.text: Check for a pre-existing install, download only from the official Microsoft Sysinternals source, install with a curated MITRE-mapped config (SwiftOnSecurity/olafhartong), wire the Sysmon + PowerShell-Operational channels into ossec.conf, validate on the dashboard.

steps.title: 2B. Linux → auditd
steps.text: Install, create identity/privilege/SSH watch rules, test with ausearch, enable realtime FIM. One real gotcha: the first touch on a monitored file before realtime FIM is enabled only becomes the baseline — it does not trigger an alert. The file has to be touched again after the agent restart to see the real detection.

steps.title: 2C. macOS
steps.text: No dedicated tooling exists here — an intentionally documented gap. macOS has neither auditd nor Sysmon, so only the native Wazuh-agent FIM is available, and it silently falls back to scheduled scanning for some folders with unexplained multi-hour detection delays.

steps.title: 3. Log it
steps.text: One line in the build log is normally enough (name, type, OS, date). A full write-up is only justified when a genuinely new error is found — not already covered by an existing guide.

steps.title: 4. (Conditional) Remove a stale agent
steps.text: Used when reinstalling on the same machine (the old manager-side registration must be removed first, or the new install fails with "Agent key already in use") or when permanently retiring a machine.

phases.title: The 17-phase build plan
phases.intro: 16 of 17 planned phases were completed (Phase 16 — physical backup media — was explicitly skipped for lack of external hardware, and documented as such rather than silently dropped). The plan itself started as a requirement-by-requirement traceability exercise — every capability named in the target role (log correlation, EDR-equivalent monitoring, a SOAR-style response layer, Python automation, network-equipment APIs) was mapped to a specific phase before any installation began, and phases 10–14 exist specifically to cover requirements that had no equivalent yet. What follows is the condensed timeline; the full narrative — including every bug — lives on the Technologies pages.
